planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Compactus' is a denser, slower-growing, more twiggy selection of burning bush than the species, reaching roughly half the ultimate size, which makes it more manageable in foundation plantings and smaller landscapes.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Compactus' is the most widely planted named selection of winged euonymus, chosen for a denser, more rounded, more twiggy habit than the species and a more restrained ultimate size, roughly 6-8 feet rather than the species' 15-20 feet. It still produces the same blazing neon-scarlet fall color and corky, wing-like stem ridges that made burning bush a landscape staple, and it still flowers and fruits, producing small orange-red berries that birds disperse. Because of this, 'Compactus' shares the species' invasive tendencies and is banned or restricted for sale in several northeastern and midwestern US states, where it has naturalized in forests and displaces native understory plants; avoid planting it near natural areas. Extremely adaptable to a wide range of soils, light conditions, and drought once established. Native alternatives with comparable fall color include highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) and black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa).

common_name: Densata Black Hills Spruce (Dense Cold-Hardy Christmas Tree Selection)

planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy or sandy, moist to average soil in full sun; Black Hills spruce is a naturally occurring, denser, slower-growing, more compact geographic form of white spruce originating in South Dakota's Black Hills, and it is exceptionally cold-hardy and wind-tolerant.

directions: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy or sandy, moist to average soil in full sun; Black Hills spruce is a naturally dense, compact botanical variant of white spruce native to South Dakota's Black Hills, distinguished from the species by tighter branching, shorter internodes, and a more uniform, symmetrical pyramidal form that requires little to no shearing. It is exceptionally cold-hardy (to zone 2), wind-tolerant, and slower-growing than typical white spruce, eventually reaching a smaller mature size. Because of its dense needle coverage and outstanding needle retention after cutting, it is considered the premium Christmas tree species for the upper Midwest and is widely planted in choose-and-cut tree farms across Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, and the Dakotas. It is also popular as a slow-growing specimen or windbreak tree where a tidier, more formal silhouette than the straight species is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil with the roots shaded and the stems in sun; 'Serotina' blooms later and over a longer season than the species, with rich purple-red buds opening to reveal creamy-yellow-throated flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone cool and shaded while allowing stems to climb toward light; 'Serotina', the classic 'Late Dutch Honeysuckle', is among the oldest and most widely grown honeysuckle cultivars, holding the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Its tubular flowers open deep purple-red to wine-red on the outside and creamy yellow within, in dense whorled clusters that are intensely fragrant in the evening, attracting hawk moths and other pollinators. True to its name, it flowers later in the season and over a longer period than the wild species, often continuing into autumn, followed by clusters of red berries that feed birds. Non-invasive, unlike the related Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), and well suited to trellises, arbors, and cottage-garden fences. Prune lightly after the main flush of flowering to encourage rebloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil with the roots shaded and the stems in sun; 'Belgica' is the earliest-blooming of the classic Dutch honeysuckle cultivars, opening reddish-purple-flushed flowers in late spring, well ahead of 'Serotina', and often reblooming later in summer.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone cool and shaded while allowing stems to climb toward light; 'Belgica', the traditional 'Early Dutch Honeysuckle', is one of the oldest named honeysuckle cultivars still in commerce, paired historically with the later-blooming 'Serotina' to extend the flowering season. Its tubular flowers open reddish-purple to rose-pink on the outside with a creamy-yellow interior, carried in whorled clusters with the same intense evening fragrance typical of woodbine, drawing hawk moths and other night pollinators. Blooming begins in late spring, noticeably earlier than the species, and plants often produce a lighter second flush later in summer. Non-invasive and well suited to arbors, trellises, and cottage-garden fences; prune lightly after the first flowering flush to tidy growth and encourage rebloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; 'Sundance' is a compact, slower-growing golden-leaved sport of Mexican orange blossom, valued chiefly for its bright yellow foliage, which colors best with some direct sun but can scorch in hot, exposed sites.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; 'Sundance' is the widely grown golden-leaved sport of Mexican orange blossom, holding the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its vivid, year-round chartreuse-to-gold foliage on a naturally compact, rounded, slower-growing habit than the green species. Clusters of small, fragrant, star-shaped white flowers appear in spring and sometimes again in fall, though flowering is generally lighter than on green-leaved forms since much of the plant's energy goes into foliage color. Best gold color develops with a few hours of direct morning sun; in hot inland climates or intense afternoon sun, leaves can bleach or scorch, so light afternoon shade is preferable in warmer zones. Like the species, it is borderline hardy at the cold edge of zone 7 and benefits from a sheltered site. Excellent as a bright foliage accent in mixed borders or containers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Aureus' is a variegated selection of Japanese euonymus with a bold yellow blotch in the center of each glossy dark-green leaf, and it colors most vividly with some direct sun, though it still tolerates considerably more shade than most variegated shrubs.

directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Aureus' is one of the classic variegated forms of Japanese euonymus, bearing thick, glossy, dark-green leaves with a bold central splash of golden yellow, the reverse pattern from gold-edged selections like 'Aureomarginatus'. The bright center coloring is most pronounced with a few hours of direct sun each day, though the shrub still tolerates considerably more shade than most variegated evergreens and remains a dependable foundation or hedge plant even under tree canopy. Like other Japanese euonymus cultivars, it is highly susceptible to euonymus scale (Unaspis euonymi); monitor regularly and treat with horticultural oil as needed. Tolerant of coastal salt spray, air pollution, and a wide range of soils, making it a versatile bright-foliage accent for shaded foundation plantings and mixed hedges in zones 6-9.
